blocks.text: A tilapia in a village pond, a goat browsing guinea grass near Kano, a red colobus in Cross River rainforest and a fiddler crab among mangrove roots in the Niger Delta are all alive — but none of them could swap places and survive. Ecology is the study of why each organism fits one place and not another, and of the living and non-living factors that make that place what it is.

blocks.markdown:
## The language of ecology

**Ecology** is the study of living organisms in relation to one another and to their environment.

A **habitat** is the particular place where an organism lives — a pond, a rotting log, the human gut, a mangrove swamp. The **niche** of an organism is its role in that habitat: what it eats, what eats it, when it is active and how it affects the others. Two species can share a habitat, but if they occupy the same niche they compete until one is excluded.

A **population** is all the members of one species living in a given area at a given time — all the *Tilapia* in one fish pond. A **community** is all the populations of different species living together in that area. An **ecosystem** is the community plus the non-living environment, interacting as a functioning unit. The **biosphere** is the sum of all ecosystems on Earth — the thin living skin of land, water and air.

blocks.title: Ecological niche
blocks.text: The functional role of a species in its habitat — its food, its predators, its time of activity and the resources it uses. Habitat is the address; niche is the occupation.

blocks.markdown:
## Abiotic and biotic factors

**Abiotic factors** are the non-living physical and chemical conditions of a habitat. **Biotic factors** are the effects of other living organisms.

Abiotic factors include **temperature**, **rainfall**, **light**, **pH**, **humidity**, **wind** and **edaphic** (soil) factors such as texture, mineral content and water-holding capacity. In the Sudan savanna around Maiduguri, rainfall is low and seasonal, humidity is low and soils are sandy; in the rainforest of Cross River, rainfall is high, light at the forest floor is dim, and soils are deep but quickly leached.

Biotic factors include **predation** (a hawk taking a lizard), **competition** (two yam plants shading each other), **parasitism** (a tapeworm in a child's intestine, or *Striga* on a millet crop) and **mutualism** (Rhizobium bacteria in the root nodules of cowpea, where both partners gain).

blocks.markdown:
## Nigerian habitats and adaptations

An **adaptation** is a feature that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its habitat.

**Tropical rainforest** (south-east Nigeria, Cross River, parts of Edo): tall trees with **buttress roots** for stability in shallow wet soil, **drip-tip** leaves that shed rain, and lianas that climb towards light. Understorey plants have large, dark-green leaves to trap the little light that reaches the floor.

**Guinea and Sudan savanna** (middle belt and north): grasses have growing points at the base, so they resprout after grazing or the dry-season bush fire. The baobab stores water in a swollen stem. Village **goats** browse a wide range of coarse plants and tolerate heat and scarce water better than cattle — they are the Nigerian equivalent of the desert camel, not the camel itself.

**Mangrove swamp** (Niger Delta, Lagos lagoon): trees such as *Rhizophora* send up **pneumatophores** — breathing roots that stick out of the waterlogged mud so the underground tissues can get oxygen. Many mangroves also have prop roots and salt-excreting glands.

**Freshwater** (rivers, oxbow lakes, village ponds): fish have gills and streamlined bodies; floating plants such as water lettuce have air-filled tissues.

In drier northern compounds, **euphorbia** and cactus-like succulents store water in swollen stems, reduce leaves to spines and carry a thick waxy cuticle — the same water-saving plan as a cactus, using plants that actually grow in Nigeria.

blocks.title: Matching an organism to its habitat
blocks.prompt: A plant growing in tidal mud along the Niger Delta has roots that project above the mud surface, and its leaves can secrete salt. Classify the habitat, name the type of root, and state whether the main limiting factor here is light or oxygen in the soil. Give one abiotic and one biotic factor that also act on this plant.

steps.text: Tidal mud that is regularly flooded is a mangrove swamp habitat, not rainforest or savanna.
Roots that stand above waterlogged mud are pneumatophores (breathing roots). They are an adaptation to anoxic soil, not to shade.
The soil is saturated, so oxygen — not light — is the factor in shortest supply around the roots. Light is plentiful on an open shoreline.

Abiotic factors here include salinity, tidal flooding, oxygen shortage in the mud, and temperature. Biotic factors include competition with other mangrove species, grazing by crabs, and mutualism with root microbes.

blocks.answer: Mangrove swamp; pneumatophores; oxygen in the soil is limiting. Abiotic: salinity (or flooding, or low soil oxygen). Biotic: competition, grazing or mutualism.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Do not use the camel as a Nigerian example. Examiners accept the goat for dry northern habitats, pneumatophores for mangrove, and basal meristems of grasses for fire-prone savanna. Habitat is where; niche is what the organism does there — mixing the two loses a mark.

points: Ecology studies organisms in relation to one another and to their environment; the biosphere is the sum of all ecosystems.
Habitat is the place; niche is the role; a population is one species; a community is all species; an ecosystem adds the non-living environment.
Abiotic factors are non-living (temperature, rainfall, light, pH, humidity, wind, edaphic); biotic factors are living (predation, competition, parasitism, mutualism).
Nigerian habitats include tropical rainforest, guinea and Sudan savanna, mangrove swamp and freshwater, each with characteristic adaptations.
Pneumatophores, savanna-grass basal meristems, goat browsing and succulent euphorbia stems are local examples of habitat adaptations.
